newsitem.title: INDIA: India gold demand rises ahead of festivals, harvest.
newsitem.headline: India gold demand rises ahead of festivals, harvest.

text.p: Demand for gold in India is expected to pick up in the coming weeks thanks to two major Hindu festivals and promising harvests after a good monsoon, dealers and analysts said on Monday.
"There's going to be a rise in demand as buying of gold is also a religious rite during festivals," said bullion analyst Madhusudan Daga.

Two Hindu festivals -- Dassera, marking the victory of good over evil, and Diwali, the festival of lights -- will be celebrated in the next 30 days. Hindus consider festivals an auspicious time to buy gold and silver.
Daga said the June-September monsoon had been widespread and extremely favourable, promising a good harvest.
"There will be money in villages and small towns to buy gold," he said. "Indians, especially in rural areas, have undying faith in gold as an investment for the future."
Daga said he expected demand for gold in India, the world's largest consumer of the precious metal, to rise by at least 5.0-7.0 percent in 1996 to about 450-475 tonnes.
In the week to Monday gold prices in Bombay, India's commercial capital and main supply centre for precious metals to other parts of the country, rose by 20 rupees per 10 grammes to 5,130 rupees.
Dealers said the end of an inauspicious fortnight as indicated by Hindu calendars had also helped prices.
"The gold market is now poised for higher seasonal demand," said bullion dealer Babubhai Jain.
Jain said the amount of smuggled gold in Bombay had fallen after recent seizures by customs officials and this had further cheered market sentiment.
Dealers estimate gold imports were around 200 tonnes in the first seven months of 1996, with 130 tonnes arriving through official channels and the remainder smuggled.
"There is a general shortage of ready stock. Prices are bound to rise further in the next few weeks," Jain said.
The impact of anticipated higher demand for gold in India has been felt at trading houses in Dubai, the feeder market for bullion on the Indian sub-continent, including Pakistan.
Dubai traders said demand from Indian expatriates as well as major Indian importers was likely to rise in the coming weeks to meet growing seasonal demand there.
"As Diwali approaches demand should be stronger for the next three to four months," one trader said.
The Indian wedding season begins soon after Diwali and Bombay traders said this could sustain gold demand for some time.
But not all that glitters is gold. Daga said high interest rates of 14-15 percent on bank deposits of one year and above were preventing investment in bullion in big cities such as Bombay.
"There's is a liquidity crunch in the big cities. Not much money is around," he said.
